tests.summary: Header: [Megamenu] Promotional tile - Authoring - What the document produces, and why position decides the variant
tests.scope: The document-to-DOM contract for the tile: the order of the slots, what an omitted optional slot leaves behind, and the rule that makes the same authored copy a light feature in one place and a dark promo in another. Also the authoring mistakes the model warns about and nothing prevents.

steps.action: Open fixture FX-01 at a desktop width above the megamenu breakpoint and expand the Products menu.
steps.result: The promotional tile renders as a dark card in the last column of the panel. Its parts appear top to bottom in this order: a plain coloured band, the eyebrow 'New Arrival', the title 'Seasonal range now in one-litre packs', then the call to action 'Explore range'.

steps.action: Still on FX-01, expand the Recipes menu instead.
steps.result: The editorial feature renders as a light card in the FIRST column of the panel, before the link columns. Its parts appear in this order: the eyebrow "Chef's Pick", the title '20-minute weeknight recipes', the description paragraph, then 'Browse recipes'. The eyebrow, title and CTA are the same three parts the promo showed, in the same order — only the surface and the extra description differ.

steps.action: On FX-01, inspect the coloured band at the top of the Products promo. The fixture's nav document authors no image and no media of any kind.
steps.result: The band is a generated element, not authored content: a span carrying aria-hidden="true" and no image inside it. Nothing an author wrote produced it, and nothing an author writes can replace it. Record this against AC-31 — the design handover specifies an authorable 16:9 image area in its place.

steps.action: Open FX-02 and expand Products. This promo authors an eyebrow and a title and no call to action at all.
steps.result: The card renders with just the eyebrow and title. There is no empty link, no empty paragraph and no reserved blank strip where the CTA would have been — the card simply ends after the title.

steps.action: On FX-02, expand Recipes. This feature authors no description.
steps.result: The title sits directly above the call to action with the normal gap between them. No placeholder text and no double gap where the description would have been.

steps.action: On FX-02, expand Training & Inspiration. This promo authors a description, which the Content Slots table gives to the feature only.
steps.result: The description paragraph does render — it is not dropped — but it carries none of the styling the feature's description has: no smaller size and no muted colour, because the promo has no rule for it. Record what it actually looks like against AC-17.

steps.action: Open FX-03 and expand Products. This fixture authors the SAME promo copy as FX-01, moved to the first row of the panel and changed in no other way.
steps.result: The identical copy now renders as the LIGHT feature card, not the dark promo: no coloured band, a pale background, and it leads the panel instead of closing it. The rest of the panel reflows around it. This is AC-13: position alone decided the variant, with nothing in the document naming either one.

steps.action: On FX-03, expand Recipes. This fixture authors the SAME feature copy as FX-01, moved to after the link columns.
steps.result: The identical copy now renders as the DARK promo card, and has gained a coloured media band it never authored. Its description paragraph is still present but, as in step 6, unstyled. Confirm that no feature-only styling survives on it and no promo-only styling appeared on anything else.

steps.action: Open FX-04 and expand Recipes. This feature's title was authored as ordinary text, without the bold the other fixtures use.
steps.result: The tile still renders and still finds a title: with no bold text to look for, the second paragraph is treated as the title. Record whether the resulting card is the one the author intended.

steps.action: On FX-04, expand Training & Inspiration. This tile authored its call to action in the row's SECOND cell instead of alongside the other paragraphs.
steps.result: The tile is not a card at all. Links in the second cell with no bold title are the signature of a labelled link column, so the whole row is classified as one: the eyebrow and title run together as the column heading and the CTA becomes a link beneath it. Nothing warns the author. Record against AC-17.

steps.action: On FX-04, expand Products. This promo authors a second call to action, which section 6 lists as a forbidden combination.
steps.result: Both links render, both styled as calls to action. Nothing suppresses the second one and nothing flags it — the constraint is documented but not enforced.

steps.action: Across FX-01 to FX-04, check every panel that has no tile left in it (Promotions, and Training & Inspiration on FX-04).
steps.result: No empty card, no stray coloured band and no leftover container appears where a tile is absent. A panel with nothing to render leaves nothing behind.

tests.notes:
Steps 6, 8, 10 and 11 record behaviour the ticket does not describe, and step 3 records a delta the ticket already flags as AC-31.

The rule behind steps 7 and 8 is worth stating plainly, because section 2 of the ticket states it differently. The ticket says the feature is the 'first non-column child'. The implementation calls the panel's first child a feature and every later child a promo, counting the link columns. Those two rules only agree when the tile is authored above the columns. Author a feature below them — which is how a document usually reads, with the editorial note last — and it silently becomes a dark promo, gains a media band, and drops its description into an element with no styling.

Step 10 is the sharper version of the same problem: the tile does not merely change variant, it stops being a tile. That row is classified by what its second cell holds, so a CTA authored one cell to the right costs the author the entire card with no error anywhere.

tests.summary: Header: [Megamenu] Promotional tile - Functionality - The call to action, and the hover and arrow the spec expects
tests.scope: Runtime behaviour on a pointer device: activating the call to action, what hovering it does and does not do, that interacting with it disturbs nothing around it, and that repeated opening of the panel does not accumulate state.

steps.action: Open FX-01 above the megamenu breakpoint with the browser console visible, and expand and collapse each of the four menus that have a panel.
steps.result: Every panel opens and closes, the tiles render inside them, and the console stays clean — no errors and no warnings raised by the header.

steps.action: Expand Products and hold the pointer over the promo's 'Explore range' link for two seconds. AC-7 expects a hover colour change here and AC-29 asks for the promo's hover to be confirmed.
steps.result: EXPECTED TO FAIL against AC-7. The link does not change colour, weight, underline or anything else on hover — no hover rule is defined for it. The design handover specifies a change to #FFA473. Record the actual behaviour.

steps.action: Expand Recipes and hold the pointer over the feature's 'Browse recipes' link. AC-7 says the feature CTA shows 'the expected hover color change'.
steps.result: EXPECTED TO FAIL against AC-7. This link does not change on hover either. The ticket flags only the promo as missing a hover rule; neither tile has one.

steps.action: With the pointer still over a CTA, compare the rest of the open panel with how it looked before.
steps.result: Nothing else moves or changes: the link columns, the other tile and the panel edges are all exactly where they were. Whatever the CTA does on hover, it does to itself and does not shift the layout.

steps.action: On FX-01, look for the trailing chevron AC-7 requires on the call to action.
steps.result: EXPECTED TO FAIL against AC-7. No chevron appears on either tile. The stylesheet no longer draws one — the arrow is now an icon the author adds — and this fixture, like the live nav, authors none. So the affordance the AC describes is absent everywhere it is not deliberately authored.

steps.action: Open FX-05, whose CTAs do author the arrow icon, and expand Products.
steps.result: A small arrow now renders after the link text, sized and aligned with it. This confirms the arrow is available but opt-in: it appears only where an author asks for it, which is the change AC-7 has not caught up with.

steps.action: Back on FX-01, expand and collapse Products ten times in quick succession, moving the pointer on and off the tile each time.
steps.result: The tile renders identically every time. There is never a second coloured band, a duplicated eyebrow or a doubled CTA, no state sticks after the panel closes, and the panel's layout does not drift.

steps.action: Inspect the promo's call to action in the DOM.
steps.result: It is a plain anchor with a real href pointing at the authored destination. It is not a button, a div or a span with a click handler.

steps.action: Read the CTA's text on its own, with none of the surrounding card visible.
steps.result: 'Explore range' and 'Browse recipes' each describe where they go without needing the eyebrow or title to make sense.

steps.action: Click the promo's call to action.
steps.result: The browser navigates to the authored href and the panel closes. Only that the navigation starts is under test here — where it lands is out of scope for this ticket.

tests.notes:
Steps 2, 3 and 5 are expected to fail as written, and all three are the same finding: the two affordances AC-7 describes are not in the code on the branch under test.

The hover is absent for BOTH tiles, not just the promo. The ticket's delta table and AC-29 flag the promo only, so the reconciliation is wider than it records.

The chevron is a different kind of absence. It used to be drawn by the stylesheet and is not any more — a comment in the code says the arrow is now an authored icon so it can be swapped or removed. That is a reasonable change, but AC-7 still describes the old behaviour, and none of the three tiles in the live nav authors an icon, so no arrow renders anywhere in production content today.

tests.summary: Header: [Megamenu] Promotional tile - Visual - Tokens, type and spacing at one desktop viewport
tests.scope: What the two cards look like at a single reference viewport, measured against the design handover and the tokens it resolves through. Breakpoints belong to the compatibility test; this one asks only whether the tile looks right where it is fully styled.

steps.action: Open FX-01 at the reference viewport and expand Products. Measure the promo card's width.
steps.result: 260px exactly. It is the panel's last column and the link columns share what is left.
steps.data: FX-01, viewport 1440x900, all measurements from computed styles

steps.action: Read the promo card's background colour.
steps.result: #221d37. This is the value AC-34 asks to be recorded as verified: the handover's own promo background resolves to the same #221D37, so there is no delta to act on.

steps.action: Read the coloured band's height and background colour.
steps.result: 106px tall, #e2dfe0. The colour matches the handover; the fixed height does not — the handover specifies a 16:9 ratio instead, which is the AC-31 delta the authoring test records.

steps.action: Read the eyebrow's colour, size, weight, letter spacing and case.
steps.result: #ff5a00, 12px, weight 600, letter spacing 0.96px, rendered in uppercase.

steps.action: Read the promo title's colour, size and weight.
steps.result: #ffffff at 24px, weight 900. Record against AC-30: the handover specifies body type here — 16px at weight 400 — so the implemented title is both larger and much heavier than the design asks for. Neither is wrong on its own; the two disagree and the ticket lists this as an open question.

steps.action: Read the promo CTA's colour, size and weight, and the padding around the card's text.
steps.result: The CTA is #ff5a00, 14px, weight 600. The eyebrow, title and CTA all sit 24px in from the card's sides; the CTA has 20px above it and 24px below. The band above them is flush to the card's edges with no padding of its own.

steps.action: Expand Recipes and read the feature card's background, title, and description colours and sizes.
steps.result: Background #f5f3f4, title #221d37 at 24px weight 900, description #5b595a at 14px.

steps.action: Read the feature's eyebrow and CTA colour.
steps.result: EXPECTED TO DIFFER FROM AC-6. Both are #b23e00. AC-6 names the project's accessible-orange, #d14900, which is not what the header uses here. Record the measured value — do not raise a defect against it without reading the note below.

steps.action: Check the divider on the feature card's inline end.
steps.result: A 1px #e2dfe0 hairline, the same divider the link columns carry, so the feature reads as the first column of the panel rather than a floating card.

steps.action: Compare the two cards for cross-contamination.
steps.result: The promo has no description styling and no light surface; the feature has no coloured band and no dark surface. Neither has picked up anything belonging to the other.

steps.action: Open FX-04 and expand Products, whose promo authors an eyebrow, a title and a CTA label all far longer than the card.
steps.result: All three wrap inside the 260px column. Nothing spills past the card's edges, nothing is clipped mid-word, no text is hidden behind a neighbouring column, and the call to action is still fully visible and clickable. The card grows taller and the panel grows with it.

steps.action: With each panel open in turn on both fixtures, check the page for a horizontal scrollbar.
steps.result: None appears at any point. The panel and its tiles stay within the page's width even with the oversized content of FX-04.

tests.notes:
Step 8 is a contradiction inside the ticket rather than a defect in the code, and a tester should not raise it as one.

AC-6 says the feature's eyebrow and CTA use accessible-orange, #d14900. AC-22 says the same text must meet AA contrast against the feature's #f5f3f4 background. Those two cannot both hold: #d14900 on #f5f3f4 is 4.08:1, below the 4.5:1 that normal-size text needs. The header defines its own #b23e00 for exactly this, which is 5.31:1 and passes, and the code says so in a comment.

So the implementation is right and AC-6 names a value that would fail AC-22. It needs correcting in the ticket, not in the code. Step 8 asserts the implemented colour so the test passes today and still catches a regression away from it.

Step 5 records the AC-30 open question with real numbers rather than restating it.

tests.summary: Header: [Megamenu] Promotional tile - Compatibility - Where the tile stops existing, and at exactly which width
tests.scope: Behaviour across viewport and input. The tile is a desktop-only element, so the question here is not how it reflows but where it disappears, whether that width is the one the spec names, and whether crossing it in either direction leaves anything behind.

steps.action: Open FX-01 at 1440px wide and expand Products, then Recipes.
steps.result: Both tiles render as fully styled cards — the dark promo in the right rail, the light feature leading the Recipes panel.

steps.action: Narrow the window to exactly 1200px and expand the same two menus.
steps.result: Both tiles are still fully styled cards. 1200px is inside the desktop treatment, not the first width outside it.

steps.action: Narrow to 1199px — one pixel below — and expand the menus again.
steps.result: EXPECTED, AND NOT WHAT THE TICKET DESCRIBES. Both tiles are gone from the rendered page entirely. The panel shows only the flattened link columns. The tiles are not restyled, not stacked and not surfaced as plain text — they are hidden outright. Record the exact behaviour; see the note.

steps.action: At 1024px — the width the design handover names as its own breakpoint — expand the menus.
steps.result: The tiles are absent, having already gone at 1200px. Record against AC-33: the implementation switches at 1200px, the handover at 1024px.

steps.action: At 900px — the width the project's own global stylesheet treats as the desktop boundary — expand the menus.
steps.result: The tiles are still absent. Three different numbers are now in play for one boundary: 1200 in the header, 1024 in the handover, 900 in the project rule and the global stylesheet. Record all three.

steps.action: At 390px, open the hamburger drawer and expand a submenu inside it.
steps.result: The submenu lists the column links. Neither tile appears in any form, and there is no empty card, stray coloured band or blank gap where one would have been.

steps.action: Resize slowly from 1199px up to 1200px and back down again, three times, with a panel left open throughout.
steps.result: The tiles appear and disappear cleanly on each crossing. On the way back up they render exactly once — never with a second coloured band or a duplicated title — and no leftover of the desktop layout survives on the way down.

steps.action: At 1440px operate the tile's call to action with a mouse; then at 390px look for any equivalent control in the drawer.
steps.result: At 1440px the CTA is hoverable and clickable. At 390px there is no CTA to operate, because the whole tile is absent — so no control is left in a state where it can be reached but not used.

steps.action: Repeat step 1 and step 6 on FX-02, whose tiles have missing optional slots.
steps.result: The same holds regardless of which slots were authored: fully styled above the breakpoint, entirely absent below it, nothing left behind either way.

steps.action: At each of 360, 390, 768, 1024, 1200 and 1440px, with every panel opened in turn, check for a horizontal page scrollbar.
steps.result: None appears at any width. Nothing in the panel forces the page wider than the viewport.

tests.notes:
Step 3 is the important one and it contradicts the ticket.

The ticket's source-of-truth table and AC-32 both say that below the breakpoint the promo's content is 'surfaced as plain stacked text and a link' inside the drawer. On develop it is not. The stylesheet hides the promo and the feature outright below 1200px, and only re-shows them inside the desktop block. Nothing is surfaced.

That matters beyond a wording correction. AC-32 asks Product and Design to decide between keeping the content surfaced, styling it, or omitting it, and marks the decision as required before development. The code has already taken the third option, which is also what the handover specifies. So the open question may be closed already — worth confirming rather than reopening.

One thing the ticket gets right that has since changed: it notes the JavaScript toggle sitting at 900px while the styling switched at 1200px. On the branch read for this plan both are 1200px, so that particular mismatch is gone and the remaining disagreement is with the handover and the project-wide rule.

This test is one test rather than a desktop and mobile pair. The two viewports are not two designs here — below the breakpoint there is no design at all, because there is no tile.

tests.summary: Header: [Megamenu] Promotional tile - Accessibility - Keyboard, semantics and contrast on both surfaces
tests.scope: Reaching and operating the call to action by keyboard, what a screen reader is given, and whether every colour pair in both cards clears WCAG 2.1 AA. Runs on the accessibility fixture, which holds the two tiles and nothing else.

steps.action: Open FX-05 at a desktop width and, using only the keyboard, reach the Products menu and open its panel.
steps.result: The panel opens from the keyboard and focus moves into it.

steps.action: Continue pressing Tab through the open panel.
steps.result: Focus reaches the promo's call to action after the link columns, matching the order the card is read in. It is reached exactly once and it is not skipped.

steps.action: Keep pressing Tab past the call to action, then press Escape.
steps.result: Focus leaves the panel and continues into the rest of the page — it is not trapped inside the tile or the panel. Escape closes the panel and returns focus to the menu's trigger.

steps.action: Tab back to the promo's call to action and press Enter. Then repeat and press Space instead.
steps.result: Enter activates the link and navigation begins. Space does not activate it — it scrolls the page, which is correct: links activate on Enter, and Space is for buttons.

steps.action: With focus on the promo's call to action, look at the focus indicator against the card's dark background.
steps.result: An indicator is visible and clearly distinguishable from the #221d37 surface. Measure its contrast against that background and record it: it must reach 3:1. Note that the header defines no focus style for this link, so whatever appears is the browser's own default — record which browser was used.

steps.action: Do the same on the feature's call to action, against the light card.
steps.result: An indicator is visible against #f5f3f4 and reaches 3:1. Record it and the browser, as in the previous step.

steps.action: Measure the contrast of the promo's eyebrow and call to action against the card background.
steps.result: #ff5a00 on #221d37 is 5.17:1 — above the 4.5:1 that normal-size text requires. Both pass.

steps.action: Measure the contrast of the promo's title against the card background.
steps.result: #ffffff on #221d37 is 16.17:1. Comfortably above the threshold.

steps.action: Measure the contrast of the feature's eyebrow and call to action against its background.
steps.result: #b23e00 on #f5f3f4 is 5.31:1 and passes. For the record: the value AC-6 names instead, #d14900, would be 4.08:1 on this background and would fail this very step — see the note on the visual test.

steps.action: Measure the contrast of the feature's title and description against its background.
steps.result: Title #221d37 on #f5f3f4 is 14.63:1; description #5b595a on #f5f3f4 is 6.29:1. Both pass.

steps.action: Measure the clickable area of each call to action.
steps.result: Record its height and width. AA requires 24x24px unless the target is inline in a sentence, which these are not — each sits alone in its own paragraph. Note the measurement even if it passes, so a later type change can be checked against it.

steps.action: Read both tiles with a screen reader, with the panel open.
steps.result: The eyebrow, title and link text are announced in the order they appear. The coloured band announces nothing at all — it carries aria-hidden and holds no text — so no phantom image or empty element is read out. Each link's accessible name is its own visible text and needs no surrounding context to make sense.

steps.action: Run axe-core on FX-05 with the Products panel open, then again with the Recipes panel open.
steps.result: No violations attributable to either tile in either state. Record anything the scan raises elsewhere on the page separately.

steps.action: Run a Lighthouse accessibility audit on FX-05.
steps.result: A score of 100, or the shortfall attributed to something outside the two tiles and recorded as such.

tests.notes:
Steps 5 and 6 are written to record rather than assert, and deliberately so. The header defines a focus-visible style for eight of its own controls and none of them is the tile's call to action, and the global stylesheet only styles focus on elements carrying a button class. So the indicator on these links is whatever the browser draws by default, which differs between browsers and is not something the project has chosen. It may well clear 3:1 in Chrome on both surfaces; that is not the same as the design having specified it. Section 2 of the ticket asserts a focus ring 'per header convention' of brand-primary at 2px with 2px offset — that convention is not applied here.

Steps 7 to 10 all pass on the branch read for this plan, and are written as plain assertions with the measured figures in them rather than as things to go and find out.

tests.summary: Header: [Megamenu] Promotional tile - Internationalization - Right-to-left mirroring and a card that cannot get wider
tests.scope: The tile in a right-to-left locale and in a language that runs longer than English. The card is a fixed 260px column whatever the language, which makes text expansion a layout boundary rather than a translation question. The panel around the tiles is Arabic too now, so the tile is judged against the columns beside it rather than against English ones.

steps.action: Open FX-06, whose page metadata sets an Arabic locale, and inspect the document element.
steps.result: It carries lang="ar-MA" and dir="rtl". The locale row is what produces both; there is no separate switch.

steps.action: Expand Products and look at where the promo card sits in the panel.
steps.result: The card has moved to the panel's left edge and the link columns run to its right — the whole panel is mirrored, and the promo is still the last column in reading order.

steps.action: Expand Recipes and look at the feature card.
steps.result: It leads the panel from the right, and its hairline divider has moved to its left side. The divider follows the reading direction rather than staying pinned to one physical edge.

steps.action: Read the eyebrow, title, description and call to action in both cards.
steps.result: The Arabic text is right-aligned and renders right to left. The four parts stay in the same order top to bottom as in English, and the padding inside the card is mirrored rather than lopsided.

steps.action: Look at the arrow icon on each call to action. Both fixtures author one.
steps.result: EXPECTED TO FAIL. The arrow still points to the right — the direction the reader has just come from — because the header stylesheet contains no right-to-left rule for it. The design handover mirrors this exact icon in right-to-left, so the intended behaviour is that it points left. See the note.

steps.action: With each panel open in turn on FX-06, check for a horizontal page scrollbar.
steps.result: None appears. Mirroring does not push anything past the page's edge.

steps.action: Open FX-07, whose locale is German and whose copy uses the long compounds German produces, and inspect the document element.
steps.result: It carries lang="de-DE" and dir="ltr".

steps.action: Expand Products and Recipes and look at both cards.
steps.result: The card is still 260px wide — it does not grow for the longer language. Every label wraps inside it, nothing is clipped or truncated mid-word, no text escapes the card, and both calls to action remain fully visible and clickable. The cards grow taller instead, and the panel grows with them.

steps.action: Check the longest single word in the German copy against the card's width.
steps.result: It fits, or wraps without overflowing the card. Record the longest word that fits, so a translator has a real number to work to rather than a guess.

tests.notes:
Right-to-left is mandatory coverage for every block in this project, and this ticket states no acceptance criterion for it — section 8 does not mention direction, mirroring or locale anywhere. Steps 1 to 6 therefore trace to nothing in the ticket and are listed under coverage gaps. Steps 7 to 9 cover the 'translated text' half of AC-15.

Step 5 is the finding. The header stylesheet has no right-to-left rules at all; it relies entirely on logical properties, which is why the cards, dividers and padding in steps 2 to 4 mirror correctly without any. That approach works for boxes and fails for glyphs: an arrow is directional content, not a margin, and no logical property flips it. The handover names this icon explicitly in its own right-to-left rule, so the design has already decided it should mirror.

The practical scope of the finding is narrow today, because the stylesheet no longer draws an arrow and no live tile authors one — the same absence the functionality test records against AC-7. It becomes visible the moment an author adds the icon the CSS is still sized for.
